steps.body: Dividing by a unit fraction asks how many of those pieces fit. 4 ÷ 1/2 means "how many halves are in 4?" Each whole holds 2 halves, so 4 wholes hold 8. That's 4 ÷ 1/2 = 8 — dividing by 1/2 gives twice as many pieces.

predict.prompt: How many halves will it take to hop from 0 all the way to 4?

options.label: 8 — two halves per whole, four wholes
2 — there are two halves in anything

predict.reveal: Each whole holds two halves, and there are four wholes to cross — so the hops multiply: 4 × 2 = 8. Dividing by 1/n multiplies by n, and the hop count is why.

widget.prompt: Hop from 0 to 4 one half at a time. The number of hops is 4 ÷ 1/2.

commonLandings.feedback: Two halves reaches only 1 whole. There are four wholes to cross, so keep going — each whole costs two hops.
Four hops reaches 2, not 4 — an easy slip, because the hop COUNT and the position look alike here. Watch the axis label, not the tally.

widget.missFeedback: Each hop is one half. Count how many it takes for the marker to reach 4.
widget.successFeedback: Eight hops. Every whole took two halves, and four wholes took eight — so 4 ÷ 1/2 = 8. That is why dividing by 1/n multiplies by n: n pieces fit inside each whole.

hints: How many halves in one whole? 2.
explanationVariants: Two halves per whole, four wholes: 8 halves.
Each whole has 4 quarters, so 3 wholes have 3 × 4 = 12.

widget.prompt: 3 ÷ 1/4: how many quarters fit in 3? (each whole has 4)

commonErrors.feedback: 7 adds 3 + 4. Count the pieces: each whole has 4 quarters, so 3 × 4 = 12.
3 is the number of wholes, not quarters. Each holds 4, so 3 × 4 = 12 quarters.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Each whole has 4 quarters, so 3 wholes have 3 × 4 = 12.

steps.body: So dividing by 1/n **multiplies** by n. It feels odd that dividing makes a bigger number, but smaller pieces means more of them fit. 4 ÷ 1/2 = 4 × 2 = 8. The rule: to divide a whole by a unit fraction, multiply the whole by the fraction's denominator.

explanationVariants: Three thirds per whole, two wholes: 6.

commonEntries.feedback: 2/3 multiplies by 1/3 instead of dividing. Dividing by 1/3 gives 2 × 3 = 6.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Each whole holds 3 thirds, so 2 wholes hold 2 × 3 = 6.
widget.successFeedback: Right — 2 × 3 = 6. Each whole holds 3 thirds, so 2 wholes hold 6.

commonEntries.feedback: 2/5 multiplies by 1/5 instead. Dividing by 1/5 gives 2 × 5 = 10.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Each whole holds 5 fifths, so 2 wholes hold 2 × 5 = 10.
widget.successFeedback: Right — 2 × 5 = 10. Each whole holds 5 fifths, so 2 wholes hold 10.

hints: How many thirds in one whole? 3.
explanationVariants: Three thirds per whole, six wholes: 18.

commonErrors.feedback: 2 divides 6 by 3. Dividing by 1/3 multiplies instead: 6 × 3 = 18.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 6 × 3 = 18 — each whole holds 3 thirds, so 6 wholes hold 18.
widget.successFeedback: Right — 6 × 3 = 18. Each whole holds 3 thirds, so 6 wholes hold 18.

takeaways: Dividing a whole by a unit fraction counts how many pieces fit.
To divide by 1/n, multiply the whole by n (the denominator).
The result is bigger than the whole — smaller pieces means more of them.
